description: We formed a team within our family to build a story telling web app for explaining about various space missions and items they left on Moon and Mars
summary:
**After the Signal** is an interactive, open-source space exploration platform that brings the stories of spacecraft, rovers, landers, and equipment left behind on the Moon and Mars to life.

Visitors can explore the solar system, navigate interactive Moon and Mars globes, and discover the journeys behind these remarkable machines—from launch and landing to scientific discoveries and their lasting legacies.

Built using NASA, JPL, ISRO, and USGS resources, our platform features **43 curated space-object records**, published mission locations, authentic imagery, and voice-guided storytelling. NASA's SPICE navigation data powers a 3D solar-system atlas, while detailed experiences, particularly Opportunity's journey, connect mission timelines, rover photographs, and exploration routes.

Our goal is to transform objects that have stopped communicating into engaging educational experiences that continue inspiring curiosity, especially among children, families, and students.

Rather than creating isolated mission presentations, we developed an extensible storytelling framework that can grow with additional missions, scientific observations, and discoveries.

Released as an open-source project on GitHub, **After the Signal turns the silent remains of space exploration into stories that future generations can continue discovering.**
details:
After the Signal is an interactive space-exploration storytelling platform that brings the forgotten stories of spacecraft, landers, rovers, and equipment left on the Moon and Mars to life.

Instead of simply displaying where a spacecraft landed, we take visitors through its journey—from launch and interplanetary travel to landing, exploration, scientific discoveries, and its lasting legacy.

Visitors can explore the solar system, select the Moon or Mars, discover objects at their recorded locations, and experience mission stories through interactive maps, timelines, original mission photographs, and voice narration.

Our initial platform includes 43 curated Moon and Mars object records, with more detailed storytelling developed for selected missions, particularly NASA's Opportunity rover.

How does it work?

The platform combines multiple publicly available scientific and historical resources from NASA, JPL, the Planetary Data System, ISRO, and USGS.

We use NASA Trek imagery to create interactive planetary globes and published mission coordinates to locate spacecraft and surface objects.

NASA's SPICE navigation data powers a 3D solar-system atlas, allowing visitors to explore planetary positions and supported spacecraft trajectories.

Selecting a mission opens its story, connecting significant events with images, scientific discoveries, and mission locations. Browser-based voice narration guides visitors through the chapters.

For Opportunity, visitors can also explore NASA rover panoramas, published traverse information, and a photographic journey assembled from 191 original mission images.

Every mission record includes supporting scientific references, while uncertain or approximate positions are explicitly distinguished from verified measurements.

What is the intended impact?

Our goal is to make space exploration understandable, engaging, and accessible to everyone, especially children, families, and students.

Space missions are often remembered through their launches or major discoveries. But the spacecraft left behind contain a much larger story of engineering, exploration, scientific achievement, and human curiosity.

We want people to understand not only where these machines are, but why they were sent, what they accomplished, what they discovered, and why their contributions still matter.

By connecting actual mission locations with visual and narrated stories, the platform makes complex scientific history easier to explore and remember.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, and software did you use?

We developed the application using JavaScript, HTML, CSS, and Node.js, supported by Python for scientific data preparation.

Our main technologies include:

  • CesiumJS for interactive Moon and Mars globes.
  • Three.js for 3D solar-system visualization.
  • NASA NAIF SPICE and SpiceyPy for spacecraft and planetary position data.
  • NASA Trek for planetary imagery.
  • NASA PDS and JPL datasets for mission photographs, rover routes, and scientific records.
  • Pannellum for interactive rover panoramas.
  • Browser speech synthesis for narrated storytelling.
  • GitHub for open-source collaboration and sharing.

Development was carried out using our personal computers, including a Mac and an NVIDIA-equipped Windows laptop for data preparation and development.

As a family team without professional software-development experience, we used OpenAI Codex and Claude as AI-assisted development tools. Our team directed the concept, storytelling approach, user experience, mission selection, and project decisions, while the AI tools assisted with coding, data preparation, research, and implementation.

How is your project creative?

Our central idea is to turn objects left behind in space into storytellers.

A discarded lander or silent rover is not merely abandoned hardware. It is physical evidence of a journey, a scientific question, an achievement, and sometimes an extraordinary survival story.

We combine interactive planetary geography, real mission navigation data, historical photographs, and narrated storytelling into a unified educational experience.

Rather than building a fixed collection of individual presentations, we created an expandable storytelling foundation. Additional missions, locations, journeys, discoveries, and scientific observations can be added over time.

The project is publicly available on GitHub so others can study, improve, and extend it.

What factors did your team consider?

Our design decisions focused on scientific accuracy, accessibility, educational value, transparency, and future expansion.

We prioritized authentic space-agency imagery and published mission records rather than invented visual evidence.

We also distinguished confirmed landing coordinates from approximate locations, actual spacecraft trajectories from illustrative diagrams, and documented rover routes from incomplete positional information.

Because this was built during a short hackathon, we concentrated on creating a working foundation and developing selected mission stories rather than claiming to cover every mission comprehensively.

Most importantly, we wanted an experience that encourages curiosity and discovery—not just passive reading.

After the Signal is our first step toward an open, interactive library of space-exploration stories, where even a spacecraft that has stopped communicating can continue teaching future generations.
